one_liner: Static trie-based range filter (SIGMOD'18); beats Bloom filters on range seeks in RocksDB, loses on point lookups.
what_it_does: SuRF is a static, one-sided-error filter built from a sorted set of byte-string keys. It answers 'might key k exist?', 'might any key fall in [lo, hi]?' and approximate range counts. A Bloom filter can only answer the first. You construct it from a sorted std::vector<std::string>, choosing a suffix type (none, hash, real or mixed) and suffix lengths, then call lookupKey, lookupRange, moveToKeyGreaterThan/moveToKeyLessThan (which return an iterator with a false-positive flag), approxCount and serialize/deSerialize. It is not a drop-in Bloom replacement: all keys must be given up front, sorted, as strings, and nothing can be inserted afterwards.
how_it_is_fast: It is built on the Fast Succinct Trie (FST), a hybrid LOUDS-DS encoding: the few hot upper levels use LOUDS-Dense (256-bit label and child bitmaps per node, so a child lookup is one array access plus a rank), and the large lower levels use LOUDS-Sparse at about 10 bits per node. Rank is a single-level lookup table over 512-bit blocks plus POPCNT, select uses a table sampled every 64 set bits, sparse-node label search compares 16 labels at a time with SSE2, and lookups prefetch across the parallel bit sequences. The filter keeps only the shortest unique prefix of each key, plus optional hashed suffix bits (fewer point-query false positives) or real key-suffix bits (these also help range queries). The RocksDB gain is avoided I/O: moveToKeyGreaterThan gives each SSTable's smallest candidate key >= the low bound without reading a data block.
when_to_use: LSM-tree or sorted-run storage (SSTables, immutable segments), where the filter is built once per file from already-sorted keys and you want to skip files on Seek. The paper measured Open-Seek at 1.5x and Closed-Seek at up to 5x over Bloom filters in RocksDB.
Time-series or event stores that often ask 'did anything happen in [t1, t2]?' and where most short ranges come back empty. The 5x gain was measured with 99% of ranges empty.
You need an approximate count of keys in a range. The code comment says it can undercount by at most 2 at the boundaries.

Static key sets of variable-length byte strings, or integers encoded big-endian with the bundled uint64ToString helper so byte order matches numeric order. Budget about 10 bits/key (random 64-bit ints) to 14 bits/key (emails) before suffix bits.
Many threads doing point lookups or iterator seeks on one shared, read-only filter. The paper's Appendix C shows point-query throughput scaling across 10 cores and 20 hyper-threads.
when_not_to_use: Point-lookup-only workloads. The paper says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'. In the RocksDB all-miss test at 14 bits/key, throughput was 32.9 Kops/s for Bloom, 19.8 for SuRF-Hash and 16.4 for SuRF-Real, because I/Os per operation were 0.022 vs 0.047 and 0.056.
Dynamic sets. The filter is static and needs a full rebuild to add keys; there is no delete. Appendix A only sketches how updates could be added.

Long keys with long shared prefixes, such as emails or URLs. The paper shows SuRF slower than Bloom on email keys and with higher false-positive rates, and SuRF-Base size has no theoretical upper bound because it depends on the key distribution.

Adversarial or key-correlated range queries, or anywhere you need a guaranteed range false-positive rate. SuRF's rate depends on the stored and queried key distributions. Later work such as Grafite (arXiv 2311.15380) targets bounded, distribution-independent range false-positive rates.

Production use without your own hardening. This is research code: x86-only (SSE2 and POPCNT hard-coded), no releases, and correctness bugs fixed as late as March 2022 (issue #13: false negatives from uninitialized label-vector tail bytes). Issue #11, a double free when destroying a deserialized SuRF, is still open. It also gives no benefit for long scans, because the paper saw no speedup on Next.

integration.dependencies: none for the filter itself (C++ standard library and SSE2 intrinsics); GoogleTest for the unit tests; YCSB, Python and the ARF git submodule for the benchmarks; the RocksDB integration lives in the separate efficient/rocksdb fork
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 with GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_popcountll, __builtin_bswap64, __builtin_ctz, __builtin_prefetch) and -mpopcnt; CMake 2.6+ for the tests and benchmarks; CI config used GCC on Ubuntu 16.04 (xenial); no MSVC support documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 only as written (unconditional <emmintrin.h> SSE2 label search, -mpopcnt required); no aarch64 or other fallback
integration.thread_safety: Building is single-threaded. lookupKey and moveToKeyGreaterThan/LessThan are const and safe for concurrent readers. lookupRange and approxCount(string, string) are non-const and reuse a member iterator, so they are NOT safe to call concurrently on one instance; the author confirmed this in issue #5. For parallel range checks, use moveToKeyGreaterThan with a per-call iterator.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — lookupKey matches a Bloom filter's may-contain semantics, but SuRF needs all keys up front as a sorted std::vector<std::string> and cannot take inserts. Using its range filtering in RocksDB needs the efficient/rocksdb fork (RocksDB 5.8 base, last pushed 2018-12), which adds Seek/SeekForPrev hooks to the filter reader interface.

gotchas: Input must be sorted in byte order, and release builds set -DNDEBUG, so nothing checks this. Issue #6 built from std::to_string(0..9999), which is not in lexicographic order, and got 9 false negatives out of 10,000. Duplicates are skipped. An empty key list or an empty-string key is only guarded by assert.

The header defines functions that are not inline (config.hpp align/uint64ToString, SuRF::create, LabelVector::search, ...). Including surf.hpp from more than one .cpp gives duplicate-symbol link errors, so wrap it in a single translation unit, as the RocksDB fork does in util/surf.cc.

Memory is managed by hand. ~SuRF() is empty, so you must call destroy() and then delete. destroy() frees the arrays but not the inner LoudsDense/LoudsSparse/bitvector objects. Copying a SuRF copies raw pointers, which leads to a double free. serialize() returns a new[] buffer the caller owns, in a raw native-endian format with no version or checksum.

The shipped defaults differ from the paper: kSparseDenseRatio is 16 (the paper says R=64, and the 64 line is commented out) and the LOUDS-Dense rank block is 512 bits, not the paper's 64. Re-tune before comparing against the published numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every sibling here (Prefix, Xor/Binary Fuse, BuRR/Ribbon, Morton, Vacuum) is a point-membership filter; SuRF is the only one that answers range emptiness, seek-to-next-key and approximate counts, so pick it only when range queries matter. For point-only filtering a sibling will be smaller and faster, since SuRF's own paper concedes point queries to Bloom.
verified_claims_summary: The SIGMOD'18 paper replaced RocksDB's Bloom filters with SuRF at equal memory (14 bits/key; SuRF with a 4-bit suffix; public efficient/rocksdb fork on RocksDB 5.8) on a synthetic 100 GB time-series (2K sensors, 128-bit keys, 1 KB values, Snappy) running on an Intel i7-6770HQ with 32 GB RAM, an Intel 540s SSD and a 1 GB block cache; compiler not stated. Open-Seek throughput went from 1.97 to 3.10 Kops/s (about 1.5x) and Closed-Seek was up to 5x faster with 99% empty ranges, but all-miss point queries fell from 32.9 to 19.8 (SuRF-Hash) or 16.4 (SuRF-Real) Kops/s; the paper measured throughput and I/Os per operation, not latency.
status_note: Abandoned (last commit 2022-03-11, no releases or tags, 4 open issues, RocksDB fork frozen since 2018-12) but Apache-2.0 (the GitHub API says NOASSERTION; LICENSE is the plain Apache text) and only about 3.5k lines across 12 headers, so it can be vendored if you accept x86-only and hand-managed memory.
